### Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

*End of phase against the historical state: POP.night_control +1 · POP.gvn_legitimacy +1 · FIND.main_force +1 · FIND.vci +1 · ARVN.effectiveness +1.*

The war that COMUSMACV inherits on 1 January 1964 is an advisory war that is being lost. Two months earlier the coup of 1 November 1963 had killed Ngo Dinh Diem and his brother Nhu, and with them went the province chiefs, the Strategic Hamlet Program and most of the administrative continuity the Republic of Vietnam possessed. The Military Assistance Command, Vietnam, under General Paul D. Harkins, is a headquarters of advisers, helicopter companies and support troops; the United States has about 23,300 military personnel in the country by the end of 1964 [H40], none of them formed into combat units, and 147 die by hostile action that year [H40]. The fighting is done by the Army of the Republic of Vietnam, the Regional and Popular Forces, and the Civilian Irregular Defense Group camps of the US Special Forces, against a Viet Cong movement that has rebuilt itself since 1959 on the political infrastructure left from the war against France and on cadres regrouped to the North in 1954 and now returning down the Trail.

Phase I runs from January 1964 to the end of July 1965. Its shape is a double collapse and a double response. In Saigon, the state comes apart: between January 1964 and June 1965 the government changes hands by coup or forced resignation repeatedly, and the generals spend more of their energy on each other than on the countryside. In the field, the Viet Cong move from the guerrilla phase to the mobile-war phase, forming regiments and then a division in the provinces around Saigon, and at Binh Gia, Song Be, Ba Gia and Dong Xoai they destroy ARVN battalions in set-piece battles. In Hanoi, the Politburo decides that the moment for decisive victory has come and commits regular PAVN regiments to the South for the first time. The American response comes in two steps: from the air, beginning with the reprisal strikes of August 1964 and February 1965 and hardening into Rolling Thunder in March 1965; and on the ground, beginning with two Marine battalions sent to guard an airfield in March 1965 and ending with the President's decision of July 1965 to commit US ground forces to the war in strength.

One thing in this phase is new. On the first day of 1964 the junta promulgates a land reform that ends rent on tenanted rice land, gives the land free to the man who works it and confirms to him whatever the Viet Minh or the Front had already given, together with an independent commission against corruption backed by an American power to suspend aid. Neither touches the main force, and the double collapse in Saigon and in the field runs much as before. What changes, slowly and only where the government holds the hamlets, is what the government's arrival means to a tenant: by the end of July 1965 about 330,000 hectares are titled [X-001], the rent stop holds in most government-held districts, and the first musters have shown the RVNAF that it is about 41,000 men smaller than its rolls [X-001]. The reforms also give the coup-makers a new grievance and Hanoi a new reason to hurry.

Every one of the political constraints that will shape the war is drawn in this phase: the restricted zones around Hanoi and Haiphong, the bar on ground operations in Laos and Cambodia, the reliance on presidential approval for targets in the North, and the decision to fight without calling up the reserves. So is the enemy's basic answer to American firepower: the decision to close in, choose the time of battle, and keep his base areas beyond the border.

A second change runs beside the first. The same decrees of 1 January gave the Republic a rural police and a system of choosing its province and district chiefs by examination, from a ranked list, for at least two years (EV002-1). Khanh's coup tested both within a month and both survived it (EV000-1). By July 1965 about 1,100 village police posts stand in the held belt, about two-thirds of the chiefs have been appointed through the list, and the Special Branch has begun to take the Front's village committees on evidence; the Front has killed about 410 constables, almost all in posts settled ahead of night security (EV002-2) [X-002]. None of it touches the main-force war or Saigon's coups.

A third change runs from the same first day, and it is a change in what this command can see rather than in what the Republic is. Two U-2S and four Global Hawks begin flying in January 1964, and the enemy's rear stops being a matter of guesswork. The coastal picket, TIDE TABLE, sees the trawlers of the North's maritime group every time they run south and closes the sea route within a year (EV003-1); Hanoi moves its southern supply to Sihanoukville about eighteen months before it did historically (EV003-2). On the night of 4 August 1964 the radar shows no torpedo boats near the destroyers, Pierce Arrow is not flown, and the Southeast Asia Resolution passes on the real attack of 2 August alone (EV000-3). The SA-2 sites are mapped as they are built, and Washington still declines to strike them (EV000-15). None of it touches the coups in Saigon, the summer offensive or the July decision.

A fourth change is in the hands of the men who fight. From January 1964 the ARVN, the Rangers, the Airborne, the Marines and the Regional and Popular Forces draw modern carbines with red-dot sights, a belt-fed squad gun in every regular squad and a marksman's rifle beside it (EV004-1). The territorials who hold the hamlets at night are no longer outgunned by the guerrillas who come over the wall, and in the held belt more posts hold through the night (EV002-2). The battles of the summer of 1965 are still lost, at Binh Gia, Ba Gia and Dong Xoai, because the enemy still chooses where and when to fight; they are lost at a smaller price, and no battalion of the general reserve is wiped out (EV000-9, EV000-17, EV000-18). The outposts that fall give the Front the same carbines.

**How the phase ends:** By the end of July 1965 the advisory war is over. The decision to commit US ground forces in strength has been taken, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and the III Marine Amphibious Force are in the country, the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) is preparing to sail, and Rolling Thunder is in its fifth month. On the other side, the Viet Cong have formed regiments and divisions in the provinces around Saigon and in the coastal lowlands, PAVN regular regiments are in the Central Highlands, and the summer offensive has destroyed ARVN battalions at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai faster than they could be rebuilt. In the countryside, the Viet Cong infrastructure administers, taxes and conscripts in a large share of the hamlets, and the government's pacification effort has nothing like the stable administration or the local security forces it needs. One thing is different from the historical summer of 1965: about 330,000 hectares of rice land have been titled to about 270,000 families, rent is no longer paid in most of the districts the government holds, and in those districts the government's arrival no longer means the landlord's [X-001]. Where the government does not hold the hamlets at night, nothing has changed except the promise.

In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta has just taken power after a year and a half of coups. In Washington, the war has an open-ended authority from Congress and a decision on troops announced without the reserves, without a tax increase and without a declaration. In Hanoi, the Politburo has committed itself to winning before the Americans arrive in strength and must now decide whether to fight them. It will: in October the PAVN regiments of the B3 Front will go after the camp at Plei Me, and the Ia Drang will follow. The war that Phase II inherits is a war between two armies that each believe they can outlast the other, fought over a population that neither government has secured.

The police and the chiefs have begun to change the same districts. About 1,100 village posts are settled, about two-thirds of the chiefs have come from the list, and the infrastructure in the villages around the posts has begun to leave them (EV002-2) [X-002]. The posts that fell were the posts settled ahead of security, and the Front has learned to kill constables before it has learned that the new chiefs are staying.

This command enters Phase II able to see the enemy's rear and not his regiments. The sea route to the coast is closed and the Cambodian route open; the Trail's first truck roads are on the U-2S's maps; the North's air defences are on its electronic order of battle; and the Southeast Asia Resolution rests on an attack that happened. The war in the hamlets and the main-force war under the canopy are exactly as hidden as before.

The rifles are in the hands of the RVNAF from the first quarter of 1964 and in all of it by the end of 1964 (EV004-1). Posts with their Popular Forces platoon now hold about nine times in ten, and the Front has turned to the posts without them, the constables on the roads, the CIDG camps and the militia, and to the mortar and the mine (EV002-2) [X-004]. The general reserve enters Phase II weakened but whole, and the Front enters it with between 10,000 and 30,000 of the Republic's carbines [X-004].

### Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

*End of phase against the historical state: POP.night_control +1 · POP.gvn_legitimacy +1 · VCI.strength -2 · FIND.main_force +1 · FIND.vci +2 · ARVN.effectiveness +1.*

Phase II is the American war at full stride. US military strength in Vietnam rises from about 184,000 at the end of 1965 to 385,000 at the end of 1966 and 486,000 at the end of 1967, and American deaths by hostile action from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966 and 9,378 in 1967 [H40]. The strategy is Westmoreland's: US divisions and brigades, with airmobility and almost unlimited firepower, seek out and destroy the enemy's main-force regiments and base areas, while the ARVN is turned increasingly to territorial security and pacification. The measure of success becomes attrition, the "crossover point" at which the enemy loses men faster than he can replace them through recruitment in the South and infiltration from the North. The instrument of measurement becomes the body count, which inflates at every level of reporting and never once establishes that the crossover has been reached.

The shape of the phase is a series of large operations that win their battles and do not change the war. At the Ia Drang in November 1965 the 1st Cavalry Division meets PAVN regulars in the Central Highlands and both sides draw the lessons they want. In 1966 the operations grow (Masher/White Wing on the Bong Son plain, Hastings below the DMZ, Attleboro in War Zone C) and in 1967 they culminate in the corps-sized sweeps of Cedar Falls and Junction City. Each kills enemy soldiers in numbers the reports exaggerate, captures rice and documents, empties villages, and is followed by the enemy's return when the Americans leave. The enemy decides when to fight; most of the large engagements begin with his attack or his ambush, and he withdraws into Cambodia, Laos and the DMZ when the cost is too high. Along the DMZ the war becomes positional: the Marines are drawn from pacification in the coastal hamlets to strongpoints at Con Thien, Gio Linh and Khe Sanh under PAVN artillery fired from the North.

Behind the main-force war, three other wars run. Rolling Thunder grows into the largest bombing campaign since 1945 against a North whose air defences grow with it, and does not stop the flow south. In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta survives the Buddhist uprising of 1966, writes a constitution and wins an election in 1967 with a third of the vote. And the pacification effort, neglected while the divisions fight, is reorganized under a single American manager, CORDS, in May 1967. In Hanoi, meanwhile, the militants around Le Duan conclude that the war of attrition is not being won either, and in the second half of 1967 they plan a general offensive to break it.

In this war a fourth runs beneath the other three, and it is the one the provisions of 1964 changed. The land programme enters the phase with about 330,000 hectares titled and leaves it with about 820,000 hectares titled to about 640,000 families, most of the Delta's tenanted rice land in hamlets the government holds at night and a great deal of the coastal Centre's [X-001]. Its first large clearing operation built around titling, GOLDEN SHEAF in the western Delta in the first half of 1966 (EV001-6), shows both what it can do and where it stops: at the edge of the territory the Regional and Popular Forces can hold after dark (F001-4). The Commission Against Corruption survives the Buddhist crisis and the election under the protection of the Aid Compliance Board, and in 1967 its Special Court convicts the first officer of general rank (EV001-7). None of this alters the main-force war, which is fought on the borders and in the Highlands where few tenant farmers live [X-001]. It alters what the main-force war is fought over.

A fifth war, the police's, runs inside the fourth. With a Special Branch that owns the files, a constable in about 1,500 villages, and chiefs who stay, the government's own belt is cleared of resident infrastructure before 1968 rather than after it: NIGHT LANTERN in Long An (EV002-4) is the case. The Front answers by killing the best chiefs (EV002-3) and by moving into the towns (EV002-5), and the police serves Ky against the Buddhists in 1966 as it served every government before (EV000-26).

A sixth war is now counted rather than guessed: the war of the enemy's rear. The Global Hawk's panhandle watch counts the trucks on the Trail through the dry seasons from December 1965 (EV003-3); the U-2S photographs the drums that made the POL strikes futile before they flew, and the Gulf watch shows within a month that they were (EV000-27); and by March 1967 MACV and the CIA agree, from the radar's count of convoys out of Kompong Speu, that Sihanoukville supplies most of the arms for III and IV Corps (EV003-4). The counts show the bombing raising the toll on the transit without lowering what arrives. They change no rule and no decision in Washington, and they find no regiment under the trees.

A seventh change is the one the soldiers notice first. Every American and South Vietnamese infantryman carries a modern carbine, every squad a belt-fed gun and a marksman, and they have done so since 1964 or since they landed. The Ia Drang and the Hill Fights cost fewer American lives, and the Marines on 881 South do not die beside jammed rifles (EV000-23, EV000-34). The rearmed Regional Forces are good enough to be borrowed by the corps, and the districts they leave pay for it (EV004-2); the cartridge cases the Front fires lead the Commission to the men who sold them (EV004-3). None of it changes who chooses the battle.

**How the phase ends:** At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 military personnel in Vietnam [H40] and has lost 9,378 of them killed by hostile action in the year [H40]. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December [H9], and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December [H39]. The enemy order of battle is in dispute: MACV counts about 300,000 communist personnel, the CIA up to 430,000 [H39], and the disagreement turns on whether the guerrillas and the political infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all.

On 21 November Westmoreland tells the National Press Club that the enemy is "unable to mount a major offensive" and that "the end begins to come into view" [H39]. The administration's progress campaign of the autumn rests on the body count, the Hamlet Evaluation System and the claim that the crossover point is near. McNamara, who has lost confidence in the war, has announced his departure for the World Bank, and Johnson's offer at San Antonio on 29 September, to stop the bombing in exchange for prompt and productive talks, has been rejected by Hanoi [H]. In Saigon there is, for the first time since 1963, an elected government under Thieu, and in the countryside CORDS has begun to organize the territorial war, from a less low base than history's. About 820,000 hectares have been titled to about 640,000 families, rent has ended in law and largely in fact wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general (EV001-6, EV001-7) [X-001]. The infrastructure of the Front is smaller in the Delta than on the historical course, and its tax take lower, but it is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, and those hamlets are still most of the contested countryside [X-001].

In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.

In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts by the end of 1967, and the arrest count has fallen because there is little left there to arrest (EV002-4, EV002-5) [X-002]. The National Police numbers about 80,000, the chiefs have mostly held their districts for two or three years, and the Front's legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less.

The enemy's external supply is measured: the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count, the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what the South's forces need from the North (EV003-3, EV003-4) [X-003]. That knowledge is honest from 1965 rather than from 1970, and it has not changed the rules, the bombing or the strategy. Its main effect on Washington has been to deliver bad news early.

The RVNAF enters 1968 with the rifles it has carried for four years and a Regional Force that the corps commanders want for their own operations, bound since 1967 by the rule that keeps it in its provinces (EV004-2). The American army has had no rifle crisis and no inquiry, and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights; it is the same army in every other respect, fighting the same battles on the enemy's terms.

### Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

*End of phase against the historical state: POP.night_control +1 · POP.gvn_legitimacy +1 · VCI.strength -2 · FIND.main_force +1 · FIND.vci +2 · ARVN.effectiveness +1.*

1968 is the year the war turns, and it turns on a battle the enemy lost. In the first hours of 31 January PAVN and VC forces attack Saigon, Hue and most of the provincial capitals of the South at once, breaking the Tet truce and every assumption of the American progress campaign. By the measures of the battlefield the General Offensive fails: there is no general uprising, the cities are retaken, Hue after a month, and the Viet Cong lose the larger part of the cadres and local forces they had built over a decade. By the measures of politics it succeeds beyond Hanoi's hopes. Within two months the President has refused Westmoreland's request for 206,000 more men, halted most of the bombing of the North, offered negotiations and withdrawn from the presidential race. US deaths by hostile action reach 14,592 in the year, the highest of the war [H40], and US strength in Vietnam stands at about 537,000 at its end [H40].

The phase has three offensives, in January–March, May–June and August–September, and three American responses. The first is military: Khe Sanh is held under the heaviest bombardment in the history of air warfare, the cities are cleared, and a new commander, General Creighton W. Abrams, takes over in June. The second is political: the decision of 31 March caps the American commitment and opens talks in Paris. The third is the countryside: with the VC's main and local forces weakened and its infrastructure exposed in the offensive, the government and CORDS move into the vacuum, with a general mobilization in June, the Phoenix programme and an Accelerated Pacification Campaign from November. The year ends with the bombing of the North stopped, a new president elected on a promise to end the war, and the war's centre of gravity shifting from the American divisions to the territorial forces and the hamlets.

The human cost in the South is the heaviest of the war to date. The offensive and the counter-attacks create about 630,000 new refugees, on top of about 800,000 displaced before; more than 70,000 homes are destroyed; by the end of the year about one South Vietnamese in twelve lives in a refugee camp [H39]. The government counts 14,300 civilian dead and 24,000 wounded in the first phase alone [H39].

In this war the year runs on the same dates and turns the same way; Tet is still decided in Saigon, Hue and at Khe Sanh, and in Washington (EV000-45) [X-001]. The difference is in the Delta and in the hamlets. The Front enters the offensive with a smaller base in the titled districts of the Bassac and the coastal Centre, recruits fewer men there in 1968 (EV000-52), and loses the towns of the western Delta faster because the hamlets around them warn the garrisons and do not hide the attackers (EV000-42). When the government and CORDS move into the countryside after the offensives, they move into hamlets where about 900,000 hectares are already titled, and the Commission audits the new Phoenix programme against the land register (EV000-54) [X-001]. The American political calendar is not changed by any of it.

The police changes Tet in the same places and in the same way: in the held belt of the Delta the Front's urban cadres are known and its guides do not arrive (EV000-42), and in Hue its lists are better because the Republic's own census fed them (EV000-44). Phoenix, here, is a new name over a Special Branch that had run target folders since 1964 (EV000-54).

Above all this the radar watches the border, and at Khe Sanh it gives the headquarters and the White House the most complete picture of an enemy concentration either has ever held, while the forces attacking the cities move among the Tet crowds where no radar can tell them from anyone else (EV000-41). After the halt it measures exactly how the North uses it (EV003-5), and Commando Hunt opens with a second ledger beside the Air Force's claims (EV000-55).

The ARVN and the territorials go into Tet with the weapons the historical ARVN received only after it. In the district towns, which the first wave attacked with local forces, about a third of the attacks never get inside the compound walls; in the cities, where the PAVN and the main force fight block by block, the rifles lower the cost and do not shorten the battles (EV000-42, EV000-44). The mobilization of June arms its new territorials from stock within the month (EV000-51).

**Events:**

**How the phase ends:** At the end of 1968 the war has changed shape without changing direction. The VC in the South have lost much of their main and local forces and many of their cadres in the three offensives, and their recruitment has collapsed; the main-force war is now predominantly a PAVN war, and the parallel administration in the hamlets, though intact in much of the country, is under more pressure than at any time since 1959. The government in Saigon has survived Tet, mobilized, and begun with CORDS to push into the countryside; ARVN units fought better in February than anyone expected, though they remain dependent on American firepower and logistics. Against these gains, the United States has decided not to escalate further and to seek a negotiated way out; the bombing of the North has ended; and the American public's tolerance for casualties, measured in a year in which 14,592 Americans died by hostile action, has been spent [H40].

In Hanoi, the leadership has paid heavily for the General Offensive and turned back to protracted war for the moment, but has won what it most needed: an American president who will not reinforce and a successor committed to withdrawal. The Paris talks exist; the shape of the table is being settled. Phase IV opens with a new administration in Washington, a war in the countryside that the South is better placed to fight than it has been for years, and an American army whose withdrawal is now a matter of timing.

In this war the countryside is better placed than that. About 900,000 hectares have been titled, the Front's Delta recruitment has fallen from a lower base, and its Delta battalions are filling with northerners earlier [X-001]. The American decision of 1968 is unchanged, and so is its timing.

The National Police numbers about 95,000 and the Special Branch has buried its first constables of the Tet battles; the infrastructure in the held belt is weaker than anywhere since 1959, and every file it keeps is now held under a destruction plan [X-002].

The enemy's rear enters Phase IV counted: the surge after the halt is measured, the first dry season of Commando Hunt is scored against the radar as well as the claims (EV003-5, EV000-55) [X-003], and the American decision of 1968 is unchanged by any of it.

The RVNAF ends 1968 larger and armed throughout with weapons the historical one was still waiting for; its new territorials have rifles and too few sergeants (EV000-51) [X-004]. The gap the rearmament opened over history is now closing from the historical side, as the M16 reaches the ARVN in 1968 and the territorials in 1969.

### Phase IV — Vietnamization and drawdown (Jan 1969 – Dec 1971)

*End of phase against the historical state: POP.night_control +1 · POP.gvn_legitimacy +1 · VCI.strength -1 · FIND.main_force +1 · FIND.vci +1.*

Phase IV is the war of the American withdrawal. US strength peaks at about 539,000 in the first half of 1969 and falls to 474,000 at the end of that year, 336,000 at the end of 1970 and 158,000 at the end of 1971 [H40]. American deaths by hostile action fall with it, from about 9,414 in 1969 [D] to 4,221 in 1970 and 1,380 in 1971 [H40]. The Republic of Vietnam's armed forces grow to replace them: from about 897,000 in 1969 to 968,000 in 1970 and about 1,048,000 in 1971–72, the territorial Regional and Popular Forces growing fastest [H62]. The policy has a name, Vietnamization, and a premise: that the South, given equipment, time and American air power, can hold what the Americans leave.

The shape of the phase is a race between the withdrawal and the South's improvement, run while Hanoi rebuilds. In the countryside, the years 1969–71 are the best the government ever has. The VC, gutted by the 1968 offensives, return to protracted war on a reduced scale; pacification spreads under Phoenix and the territorial forces, into a countryside where the land programme of 1964 has already done most of its work (the Land to the Tiller law of 1970 does not happen, EV000-65); and by most indicators, including the ones the enemy cannot fake, the VC's hold on the population of the Delta and the coastal lowlands weakens. On the frontiers the war goes the other way. The North rebuilds its main forces, extends the Trail and its pipeline, and after Sihanouk's fall loses Sihanoukville but gains much of eastern Cambodia. The United States uses the time it has to strike the sanctuaries it had left alone, secretly from the air over Cambodia from March 1969, on the ground in Cambodia in May–June 1970, and through the ARVN alone in Laos in February–March 1971, and Congress closes the ground option behind each attempt.

At home the war's support is gone. The revelation of My Lai, the Moratorium, the Cambodian incursion and Kent State, the trial of Calley and the publication of the Pentagon Papers mark a country that wants its army home, and an army in Vietnam, after 1969, that is itself coming apart under drugs, racial conflict and attacks on its own officers, waiting to leave a war it no longer expects to win [H]. In Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh dies in September 1969; the collective leadership around Le Duan negotiates secretly with Kissinger and, after the ARVN's defeat in Laos in 1971, decides to try once more for victory by conventional invasion.

In this war the phase follows the same course on the frontiers and in Washington [X-001]. In the countryside it starts further on. The land programme has nothing left to do by 1970 but the communal lands, and about 1,150,000 hectares are titled by the end of 1971 [X-001]. The Commission Against Corruption, which had outlived three governments behind the American lever, loses that lever as the Americans leave, and in July 1971 Thieu puts it under a presidential inspectorate after it opens an inquiry that reaches his own circle (EV001-8) [X-001].

The police and the provinces end the phase as the Commission does: their work below the palace goes on, and their reach upward ends as the American lever lapses (EV002-6). The historical gap narrows, because the Republic builds after 1968 what this war had from 1964.

The enemy's rear is counted through the whole phase. The Cambodian incursion goes in on a map five years in the making and finds the caches in days rather than weeks, though Washington still names COSVN as the objective (EV000-66); Commando Hunt's claims are checked every night against a radar count, and the claim that the trucks destroyed exceeded the trucks that existed never survives a season (EV000-68); and Lam Son 719 goes in with an honest estimate of what waits for it, and fails for the reasons it failed historically (EV000-71).

**How the phase ends:** At the end of 1971 the United States has about 158,000 military personnel in Vietnam, its ground combat role is nearly over, and the last US combat divisions are leaving [H40]. The RVNAF numbers more than a million men under arms, well equipped and, in the territorial forces, more present in the hamlets than ever before [H62]. In the countryside the VC remain weaker than at any time since 1960 and weaker in the Delta than on the historical course; the land programme of 1964 has finished its work, with about 1,150,000 hectares titled, and the Land to the Tiller law of 1970 was never needed (EV000-65) [X-001]. The Commission survives below the rank of minister and general and no longer above it (EV001-8) [X-001]. These gains are real, and they are measured mostly by indicators the government itself produces.

On the frontiers the balance is the reverse. The PAVN has rebuilt its main forces, extended the Trail in Laos and Cambodia, lost Sihanoukville and replaced it, and watched the ARVN's best divisions fail in Laos without American advisers. The secret channel in Paris is deadlocked on Thieu's removal and on the PAVN's presence in the South. In Hanoi, after Lam Son 719, the Politburo has decided to stake the next year on a conventional invasion across the DMZ, from Laos into the Central Highlands and from Cambodia towards Saigon, timed to an American election year and to the near completion of the American withdrawal [H56] [H]. The question of Phase V is the one Vietnamization was built to answer: whether the South can stop a PAVN conventional offensive with American air power but without American ground troops.

The Board still ranks the candidates and the Prime Minister now chooses the loyal among the competent (EV002-6) [X-002]. The posts, the census and the district Special Branch sections stand, and the historical police has caught up with them in size; what the Republic keeps from 1964 is the chiefs' experience and four extra years of files.

The radar's ledger has made the interdiction debate honest and changed nothing it was about: the Trail is larger at the end of 1971 than ever, the Liberation Route through northeastern Cambodia is mapped and open, and the aircraft that count both will leave with the Americans (EV000-68) [X-003].

### Phase V — The Easter Offensive and Linebacker (Jan 1972 – Dec 1972)

*End of phase against the historical state: FIND.main_force +1.*

1972 is the test of Vietnamization, and the answer it gives is exact: the Republic of Vietnam can stop a full PAVN conventional offensive with American air power and American advisers, and cannot do it without them. On 30 March the PAVN opens the largest offensive of the war, called the Nguyen Hue Offensive in Hanoi and the Easter Offensive in the West, with about fourteen divisions and hundreds of tanks [H] on three main fronts: across the DMZ into Quang Tri, from Laos and Cambodia into the Central Highlands at Kontum, and from Cambodia down Route 13 at An Loc towards Saigon [H64]. US ground strength has fallen to about 69,000 men, few of them combat troops, and is on its way to 27,000 [H64]. US air power returns in strength: B-52s and tactical aircraft over the battlefields of the South, and, for the first time since 1968, a bombing campaign against the North without most of Rolling Thunder's restrictions, with the mining of Haiphong.

The shape of the phase is a near-collapse in the spring and a recovery in the summer. Quang Tri Province falls on 1–2 May; Kontum and An Loc are besieged and held by narrow margins and B-52s; and by the autumn the ARVN, under better commanders, has retaken Quang Tri City. The PAVN loses most of the armour it committed and, by most estimates, about 100,000 men, killed and wounded, while keeping about a tenth of the South's territory, mostly thinly populated border regions in the west [H64]. The offensive creates almost a million refugees and kills more than 25,000 civilians [H64]. Its political result is the one Hanoi needed: a settlement on terms that leave PAVN troops in the South. The year ends with the October draft agreement, Thieu's refusal of it, and the eleven days of Linebacker II.

In this war the armour of the Easter Offensive is seen before it crosses the DMZ and is struck by radar-bombing B-52s through the cloud that grounded the fighter-bombers (EV000-74); Linebacker chooses from target folders seven years in the making and counts the effect of the mining on the North's own roads (EV000-75); and at An Loc the B-52 boxes of 10–12 May fall on assembly areas the radar shows (EV000-76). Quang Tri still falls, An Loc and Kontum still hold, and the lessons both sides draw are the historical ones.

**How the phase ends:** At the end of 1972 the war is on the verge of a settlement that both governments in Vietnam regard as provisional. The Easter Offensive has failed to destroy the ARVN or the Thieu government, at a cost to the PAVN of most of the armour it committed (by one count 134 T-54s, 56 PT-76s and 60 T-34s) and about 100,000 men [H64]. The ARVN has held at An Loc and Kontum and retaken Quang Tri City, but has lost Quang Tri north of the Thach Han, the western Highlands and the border areas of III Corps, and its losses are given variously from about 10,000 killed to about 39,000 dead in the period [H64]. Almost a million South Vietnamese have been made refugees, about 600,000 of them in government camps [H64].

The lesson both sides draw is the same. The ARVN held where American air power was decisive, at An Loc and Kontum, and where American advisers coordinated it; it broke where its leadership failed, at Quang Tri and Tan Canh. The settlement about to be signed removes the American advisers and the American air power and leaves the PAVN in the South, while the North's air defences and economy recover. Hanoi needs only to rebuild, wait for the Americans to be gone, and choose its time.

The aircraft are still flying at the end of 1972, still American, and under the agreement about to be signed they will soon have no American strike force to cue. The Republic keeps nothing of them: no aircraft, no exploitation cells, no practice in using either.

### Phase VI — Paris, the endgame, and 1975 (Jan 1973 – Dec 1975)

*End of phase against the historical state: as historical on every headline variable.*

Phase VI is the war without the Americans, and the end of the Republic of Vietnam. The Paris Agreement of January 1973 takes US forces out and returns the prisoners; it leaves the PAVN in the South, the Thieu government in Saigon, and the war to be decided between them. The ceasefire never holds. In 1973 Saigon is on the offensive, recovering hamlets and roads, while the North rebuilds; in 1974 the two are evenly matched, and the ARVN, short of ammunition, fuel and spare parts as American aid falls, bleeds in a war of attrition it cannot sustain; in January 1975 the North tests whether the United States will respond to the seizure of a province, and when it does not, it commits everything [H72].

The shape of the phase is three slow years and seven fast weeks. The constraints that bind the American role are now law, not policy: the Case–Church amendment ends all US combat activity in Indochina from 15 August 1973, the War Powers Resolution limits the President's power to send forces back, and Congress cuts military aid. Watergate removes the President who gave Thieu his assurances. In Hanoi, the 21st Plenum of October 1973 returns to revolutionary violence, and the PAVN builds a road network east of the mountains, a fuel pipeline into the South and an army of corps. In Saigon, the economy, hit by the oil shock and the departure of the Americans whose spending had sustained it, and a government that has narrowed its base, face the offensive of 1975 with an army spread thin across the whole country. When the blow falls at Ban Me Thuot in March, Thieu's decision to abandon the Highlands turns a defeat into a rout, and in eight weeks the Republic falls. The PAVN enters Saigon on 30 April 1975.

In this war the army that fights the last three years has been built for ten years around the belt-fed gun and the abundance of American ammunition, and the ration of 1974 finds it more dependent on volume than the historical one (EV000-89). It fights the attrition of 1974 and the stand at Xuan Loc with better weapons than its enemy and too few rounds to use them, and the hoards it builds against the ration are lost with I Corps (EV000-91, EV000-96).

**How the phase ends:** The war ends on 30 April 1975 with the fall of Saigon and the unconditional surrender of the Republic of Vietnam, on the historical timeline: rung (a), collapse. The Paris Agreement had removed the American forces and kept the PAVN in the South; Congress had written the end of American combat and the limits on the President into law; American military aid had fallen; and the government in Saigon, more stable than at any time since 1963 but narrowly based, economically weakened and dependent on American supply, faced an enemy that had rebuilt after 1972 and chose its moment. The decisive blows were Hanoi's, at Phuoc Long and Ban Me Thuot; the decisive errors were Saigon's, in the order to abandon the Highlands and the contradictory orders to I Corps.

Hanoi's posture never changed. It was committed to armed reunification throughout, from the Ninth Plenum of December 1963 to the Ho Chi Minh Campaign, through the losses of 1965–68 and 1972, and it accepted the Paris Agreement as a step towards that end. The US war in Vietnam, from the advisory years to 1973, cost more than 58,000 American dead [H]. The Vietnamese dead, military and civilian, northern and southern, are counted in the millions by most estimates, and the record of them is less precise than the record of the Americans [H]. That is the war as it happened, and the war the exercise begins from.

The squad guns and the marksmen's rifles of the ARVN, and about 9 million rounds of linked 5.56mm from the divisional hoards of I and II Corps, are in the PAVN's hands by the end of April 1975, with the carbines of a million men [X-004].

# Card 005 — B-52J Stratofortress replacing every B-52, with GBU-31 and GBU-38 JDAM and Quickstrike mines

*Memorandum 005 · status part2 · full record: memos/005/ · generated by fie.py*

## P005a · Boeing B-52J Stratofortress, programme-of-record configuration: B-52H airframe re-engined with eight Rolls-Royce F130 turbofans (Commercial Engine Replacement Program), Raytheon AN/APQ-188 AESA radar (Radar Modernization Program), digital cockpit displays, 1760 Internal Weapons Bay Upgrade, GPS-aided navigation and the H's electronic-warfare suite, replacing every B-52 one for one
Every B-52 in the USAF inventory replaced one for one [U]: about 600 airframes in 1964 across SAC [E: 744 B-52s built, less attrition and retirements of early B and C models], of which the force committed to Southeast Asia follows the historical deployment: 30 in mid-1965 [H], about 50–70 through 1966–67 [E: sortie rates of about 800 a month by mid-1967 per S9], about 90–100 from early 1968 [E: 1,800 sorties a month from February 1968 per S9], 210 at the 1972 peak [M005·S9] · spaces 0 in RVN for the bomber force itself [E: Arc Light flew from Guam, U-Tapao and Okinawa]; about 40 in RVN for an enlarged Arc Light liaison and target-coordinate cell at MACV and Seventh Air Force [E: the historical ARC LIGHT liaison element plus a coordinate-mensuration team]; outside RVN, maintenance manpower about 10–20% below the historical B-52 force [E: F130 needs no off-wing overhaul per S4, five-man crew per S2 against the D's six] · arrives 1964-01-01 · STRIKE, INTERDICT, FIX, SUSTAIN · air

**Key figures.**
- Programme status: CERP Milestone B 1 June 2026; AN/APQ-188 Milestone C 21 August 2026; IOC mid-FY2033 [M005·S1] [M005·S3]
- Crew: 5 (no tail gunner) against the B-52D's 6 [M005·S2] [H]
- Payload: about 70,000 lb mixed ordnance [M005·S2]
- JDAM load: 20 (8 internal, 12 external) [M005·S6]; GBU-38 about 30–40 [E: D3]; unguided Mk 82 about 51 [E: D3] against the Big Belly's 108 [M005·S9]
- Speed 650 mph (Mach 0.86); ceiling 50,000 ft [M005·S2]
- Range: H 8,800 miles unrefuelled [M005·S2]; J estimated 10,500–12,000 miles [E: F130 about 30% more fuel-efficient, S4]
- Guam–South Vietnam round trip unrefuelled with full conventional load [E: D5 range estimate]
- Maintenance manpower about 10–20% below the historical B-52 force; no F130 off-wing overhaul [E: D2 and S4] [M005·S4]
- Estimated loss rate over Hanoi a third to a half of the historical Linebacker II rate of 15 in 729 sorties [E: D7] [H]
- In-theater strength follows history: 30 in 1965, 210 at the 1972 peak [H] [M005·S9]

**Negative specification.** The B-52J finds nothing under canopy: its AN/APQ-188 radar and targeting pod see bridges, ferries, roads and open ground, not regiments under triple canopy, and it addresses neither half of the find-and-fix problem (A6). It is not a better carpet-bomber: it carries about 51 unguided 500 lb bombs [E: the B-52H conventional load in D3] against the Big Belly B-52D's 108 [M005·S9], so an Arc Light box flown by Js with unguided bombs is half as dense. Its precision lives entirely in its GPS weapons and in the coordinates fed to them; no 1965 ground unit can pass it a digital coordinate or read a grid reference finer than about 100 m [E: 1:50,000 map reading to six figures]. It does not escape the SA-2 over Hanoi, whose engagement range of about 25 miles [E: published SA-2 engagement envelope] exceeds the JDAM's 15-mile glide [M005·S7]. It is not in service in 2026: its performance figures are the B-52H's plus programme claims [M005·S1] [M005·S3]. It does not transfer to the VNAF. It does not lift any political constraint: where it may bomb is still decided in Washington.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the protection of weather and of distance from base, since GPS weapons fall through the monsoon and the bomber reaches any target unrefuelled from Guam. Against fixed targets, it denies the enemy safety in point defences, since GPS weapons can be released up to 15 miles outside them [M005·S7]. It denies him the habit of reading Arc Light's intentions from the tanker rendezvous [E: the tanker rendezvous was visible to the trawler off Guam, S9].

**Verdict.** The B-52J is a better aircraft than the B-52D in almost every respect that can be measured: it burns about 30% less fuel [M005·S4], flies to the South from Guam without tankers [E: D5 range estimate], risks five men instead of six [M005·S2], and carries twenty 2,000 lb GPS weapons [M005·S6] where the D carried none. But the war Arc Light fought was a war of area bombing on targets located by intelligence hours or days old, and for that war the J is a worse carpet and an equal guess. Its real value is the GBU-31 and GBU-38 it carries, and their value depends on coordinates: on the U-2S and the Global Hawks of Memorandum 003, and on what the ground war can locate. Where Washington lets it strike fixed targets in the panhandle and the North, the J is a transformation of what one bomber can destroy in one night in any weather. In the South, against an enemy under canopy who chooses when to fight, it is a more efficient way to do what the D did.

**Pushes:** STRIKE.responsiveness +1, AIR.losses -1, AIR.north_effect +1 · **Depends on:** FIND.main_force, AIR.north_defences, US.political_tolerance, INTEL.penetration

## P005b · GBU-31 Joint Direct Attack Munition, 2,000 lb class: GBU-31(V)1/B on the Mk 84 general-purpose bomb and GBU-31(V)3/B on the BLU-109 penetrator, Boeing GPS-aided INS tail kit, with FMU-152 or equivalent programmable fuze, 2026 configuration
Supplied with the B-52J force at realistic production rates [U]: about 8,000–12,000 kits a year from 1964 for the bomber force [E: about a third of a JDAM production line of 25,000–40,000 kits a year, the rest going to the GBU-38 and to stocks] · spaces ~60 in RVN [E: a coordinate-mensuration and weaponeering cell at MACV J-2 and Seventh Air Force working in shifts]; kit build-up and loading crews of about 150–250 at Andersen and U-Tapao outside RVN [E: munitions maintenance squadron increments] · arrives 1964-01-01 · STRIKE, INTERDICT · air

**Key figures.**
- Weights: GBU-31(V)1/B (Mk 84) 2,036 lb [M005·S7], GBU-31(V)3/B (BLU-109) 2,115 lb [M005·S7]
- CEP 5 m or less with GPS; 30 m or less for 100 s without GPS; 9.6 m in operational test [M005·S7]
- Range up to 15 miles; release up to 45,000+ ft [M005·S7]
- B-52J load: 20 (8 internal, 12 external) [M005·S6]
- Mk 84 fill about 945 lb [E: published Mk 84 fill]; BLU-109 penetrates about 1.8–2.4 m reinforced concrete [E: D3]
- Supply to theater about 8,000–12,000 kits a year [E: D1], enough for about 400–600 full sorties a year [D]
- Coordinate cell about 60 men at MACV J-2 and Seventh Air Force [E: D2]; 1:50,000 map coordinates in the mountains 100–300 m off [E: D2]
- Kit cost about $22,000 (FY2007) [M005·S7]

**Negative specification.** The GBU-31 has no seeker and finds nothing: it goes to a coordinate and cannot follow anything that moves. Its accuracy of 5 m or less [M005·S7] is relative to the coordinate given, and in 1965 the best coordinate available is a map grid with errors of 100–300 m in the mountains [E: D2], unless the U-2S and Global Hawk imagery of Memorandum 003 is measured to produce it [M003]. It cannot equip Arc Light: about 8,000–12,000 kits a year [E: D1] support about 400–600 full sorties a year [D] against up to 1,800 Arc Light sorties a month [M005·S9]. The BLU-109 penetrates about 1.8–2.4 m of reinforced concrete [E: D3] and does not reach the deep levels of tunnel systems 3–10 m down in laterite [E: D3]. It cannot be released by any VNAF aircraft, none of which has a 1760 interface. It changes no political constraint: the bridges of the North can be struck only where Washington allows.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the protection of weather over his fixed targets, and the safety of point defences around them. It also denies him the safety of numbers: a bridge that survived hundreds of unguided bombs now falls to a handful. Fixed infrastructure with a known coordinate becomes untenable, which pushes the enemy towards infrastructure he can move, hide or rebuild overnight.

**Verdict.** The GBU-31 makes every fixed target with a measured coordinate a target that dies in one strike, in any weather, from 1965. That changes the air war against bridges, ferries, depots, power plants and fortified positions as completely as the laser-guided bomb changed it in 1972, and seven years earlier. It does not change the war against an enemy whose valuable things are not fixed: men, trucks under trees, rice in caches and regiments in the forest. Its value in the South is limited by the coordinate, and in the North by Washington. Its supply limits it to a precision force inside Arc Light, not a replacement for it.

**Pushes:** AIR.north_effect +1, TRAIL.capacity -1, POP.civilian_harm -1, INTL.communist_aid +1 · **Depends on:** FIND.main_force, TRAIL.capacity, INTL.chinese_intervention_risk, AIR.north_defences

## P005c · GBU-38 Joint Direct Attack Munition, 500 lb class: Boeing GPS-aided INS tail kit on the Mk 82 or BLU-111 bomb body, with FMU-152 or equivalent programmable fuze, 2026 configuration
Supplied with the B-52J force at realistic production rates [U]: about 15,000–25,000 kits a year from 1964 [E: the larger share of a JDAM production line of 25,000–40,000 kits a year] · spaces ~0 additional in RVN [E: shares the P005b coordinate cell]; about 100 loaders and kit builders outside RVN [E: the 500 lb kit's higher count per sortie] · arrives 1964-01-01 · STRIKE, FIX · air

**Key figures.**
- Weight 558 lb (Air Force) or 590 lb (Navy) on Mk 82/BLU-111; length 92.6 in [M005·S7] [M005·S8]
- CEP 5 m or less with GPS; range up to 15 miles; release up to 45,000 ft [M005·S7]
- B-52J load about 30–40 [E: §1.1 D3]
- Mk 82 fill about 190 lb [E: published Mk 82 fill]
- Danger-close for a 500 lb bomb about 400 m in the open [E: danger-close tables]; historical Arc Light safety distance 3 km, later about 1 km [E: Arc Light safety distances at Khe Sanh and An Loc]
- Supply to theater about 15,000–25,000 kits a year [E: D1]; about 400–800 full sorties a year [D]
- Guided sorties of both sizes about 800–1,400 a year against Arc Light's 800–1,800 a month [D] [M005·S9]
- 1965 ground coordinate by map about 100 m accuracy [E: 1:50,000 map reading]

**Negative specification.** The GBU-38 has no seeker and cannot follow a moving target; the Laser JDAM that can is not supplied [M005·S8]. Its CEP of 5 m or less [M005·S7] applies to the coordinate it is given, and the 1965 infantryman, controller or forward observer can give a coordinate only to about 100 m by map [E: 1:50,000 map reading], because no historical ground unit has a GPS receiver (CONFIG conditions). It is not an artillery substitute for the minute-to-minute fight: it comes when a B-52J is overhead and cannot be adjusted. It does not defeat the enemy's hugging tactics; it narrows the gap he must close. Danger-close for a 500 lb bomb remains about 400 m in the open [E: danger-close tables for 500 lb bombs]. A wrong coordinate near a perimeter is a precise fratricide. Supply supports about 400–800 full sorties a year [D]. It cannot be released by any VNAF aircraft.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the time and safety to dig siege works within a kilometre of a besieged base: positions he holds long enough to be measured can be struck one by one, at night and in cloud, a few hundred metres from the defenders. It narrows the safety margin his hugging tactics depend on, and it denies him safety for trucks, guns and parks in the open whose positions are known.

**Verdict.** The GBU-38 gives the B-52 something it never had: the ability to put 30–40 separate 500 lb bombs on 30–40 known positions near friendly troops, in any weather [E: §1.1 D3 carriage]. In the sieges of this war, at Plei Me, Con Thien, Dak To, Khe Sanh, Kontum and An Loc, where the enemy closed on a fixed position and dug in long enough to be measured, that is a large change in what the bombers can do for the men inside the wire. Elsewhere it is limited by the 1965 infantryman's map, by the enemy's choice to fight where he cannot be measured, and by supply.

**Pushes:** FIX.capability +1, US.casualties -1, POP.civilian_harm -1, ENEMY.engagement_control -1, ARVN.self_sufficiency -1 · **Depends on:** FIND.main_force, STRIKE.responsiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control

## P005d · Quickstrike family of aircraft-laid bottom influence mines: Mk 62 (500 lb), Mk 63 (1,000 lb) and Mk 64 (2,000 lb) on Mk 80-series bomb bodies, Mk 65 (2,000 lb class thin-walled case), and Mk 64 Mod 5 Quickstrike-ER with the JDAM-ER wing kit, with Mk 57 and Mk 71 target detecting devices (magnetic, seismic, pressure and acoustic), 2026 configuration
Supplied with the B-52J force at realistic production rates [U]: about 3,000–6,000 mines a year from 1964, of which a few hundred Quickstrike-ER [E: conversion kits on existing bomb bodies, with target detecting devices the rate limit; QS-ER still in demonstration per S15] · spaces ~0 in RVN [E: assembly and preset at Guam and U-Tapao]; about 40–60 Navy mine assembly and preset specialists outside RVN [E: a Mobile Mine Assembly Group detachment] · arrives 1964-01-01 · INTERDICT, STRIKE · naval

**Key figures.**
- Family: Mk 62 (500 lb), Mk 63 (1,000 lb), Mk 64 (2,000 lb) bomb-body mines, Mk 65 (2,390 lb, depths to 600 ft), in service 1983 [M005·S11] [M005·S13]
- Quickstrike-ER: Mk 64 with GBU-64v1 JDAM-ER kit, released more than 40 miles out; 12 per B-52H pending certification [M005·S15]
- Standard laying below about 500 ft at about 300 knots or less [M005·S14]; B-52 from about 1,000 ft at 500–600 km/h [M005·S16]
- Detecting devices: Mk 57 and Mk 71 (magnetic, pressure, seismic, acoustic; ship classification) [M005·S12] [M005·S16]
- B-52J loads: about 51 Mk 62 [E: §1.1 D3]; about 20 Mk 64 or Mk 65 [E: §1.1 D3]
- Supply about 3,000–6,000 mines a year, a few hundred ER [E: D1]
- Haiphong mining prohibited until May 1972; 27 ships stayed in Haiphong after the May 1972 mining [H] [M005·S17]
- Fill: Mk 62 about 190 lb, Mk 63 about 445 lb, Mk 64 about 945 lb [E: published Mk 80-series fills]

**Negative specification.** Quickstrike does not detect wooden sampans, bamboo rafts or floating drums: its magnetic setting ignores them, and pressure or seismic settings may catch only the larger wooden junks [E: pressure signatures of larger hulls]. It does not close the Trail: it closes waterways, and the historical Destructor fields of 1965–68 in the panhandle did not stop the flow [M005·S17]. It cannot be laid in Haiphong or the northern ports before May 1972, nor in Cambodian waters, under the modelled constraints [H]. Standard Quickstrikes are laid at 500–1,000 ft [M005·S14] [M005·S16], which over defended crossings means AAA; safe laying needs the Quickstrike-J or the Quickstrike-ER, which is still in demonstration in 2026 [M005·S15]. Its fields need reseeding every few weeks [E: D10] and cannot be switched off after laying. Its value against land vehicles is not established in my sources.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the use of steel-hulled craft on mined waterways and coastal approaches south of the 20th parallel, and the use of Haiphong from May 1972, without sweeping or loss. It forces him onto wooden craft, roads and trucks. It denies him safe passage at the ferries and fords where boats and barges must cross.

**Verdict.** Quickstrike is a better Destructor and a better Mk 52. Its greatest use in this war, the closing of Haiphong, is prohibited until May 1972 by Washington, and when it comes the historical mines did the job. In the panhandle's rivers and coastal lighterage it raises the toll on the North's waterborne logistics from 1965 and forces the load onto wooden craft and trucks, but it does not reduce what arrives in the South by much, because the Trail has the road. It is a modest provision on its own and a valuable one only if Washington lets it be used against the ports.

**Pushes:** TRAIL.tonnage_arriving -1, AIR.north_effect +1 · **Depends on:** INTL.communist_aid, INTL.chinese_intervention_risk, SANCT.laos, SANCT.cambodia, TRAIL.capacity

EC005-1 the precision cell inside Arc Light · EC005-2 the bridge night · EC005-3 the siege box (with P003b) · EC005-4 the high orbit · EC005-5 the navigated carpet · EC005-6 the estuary field (with P003b) · EC005-7 the Laotian river crossings · EC005-8 the Haiphong plan in the drawer (May 1972) · EC005-9 the fixed-target strike in the North. Abandoned: EC005-10 hunting trucks by radar (precision in space, not time) · EC005-11 close support by voice grid (map error and datum; precise fratricide) · EC005-12 low-level mine laying by B-52J (flak) · EC005-13 bunker-busting in the tunnels (too shallow; no coordinates)

- P005d × P003b: the Gulf watch and the panhandle watch count the traffic on the mined rivers and estuaries, see sweeping begin, and cue reseeding; the mine's effect is measured, not claimed

- **POSTNA-5** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.credibility_gap, US.casualties · The American political clock is spent by casualties, cost and time, and fastest by the discovery that reported progress was false; a provision that improves a metric without improving the war shortens the clock (TNA G-5, G-10)
- **POS003-1** · vars: FIND.main_force, FIX.capability, STRIKE.responsiveness · Airborne radar and signals reconnaissance find the enemy's movement in the open and his headquarters' transmitters, never his regiments under canopy; their value in any engagement equals what can be put on a track within the hour, and an improvement in finding is never claimed as an improvement in fixing (003 §2 F003-5; §4.P2–P5)
- **POS003-2** · vars: INFIL.sea, SANCT.cambodia, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving · In this war the sea route to the South's coast closed in 1964 under observation and the enemy's southern supply moved to Sihanoukville from June 1965; supply through Cambodia, not by sea, is the principal external line into III and IV Corps from 1965 until Lon Nol's coup (003 §2 F003-3; EV003-2)

- **POS004-1** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, ENEMY.engagement_control · Infantry small arms change how the fights the enemy accepts go, never which fights he accepts; at the outpost their value equals the platoon's presence after dark and the reaction behind it, and the enemy's answer to a better-armed post is to attack what is not rearmed (004 F004-1, F004-3, F004-16; §4.P1)
- **POS004-2** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance · In this war the ARVN and the RF/PF carry modern carbines from 1964, and the 1967 M16 crisis and inquiry and the 1968–69 rearmament do not occur; from 1969 the historical army has caught up, and the remaining difference is the squad gun, the marksman and the practice (004 F004-6; §4.P2–P4)

## Trajectory Log — last 5 entries

## Memo 001 — Accelerated land-to-the-tiller reform and an enforced GVN anti-corruption programme

Memorandum 001 gave the Republic land reform and an anti-corruption commission on the war's first day. The war's interior moved; its outline did not. About 1,150,000 hectares were titled by 1971, six years ahead of history, and where the government held the night its arrival became a guarantee rather than the landlord's return: the Delta's Front recruited less, filled its battalions with northerners sooner and in 1969 conceded the land issue. The Commission counted the army honestly, convicted a general and audited Phoenix, then lost its American lever with the drawdown and was curbed in 1971. Every main-force battle, Tet's political verdict, the Easter Offensive and the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 stand. The end state stays at rung (a). The provisions first touched G-1, the political deficit, and showed that moving it is necessary but not sufficient: a South with more to hold still needs the means to hold it against a conventional invasion after the Americans leave.

## Memo 002 — National Police reform with a rural constabulary, and merit-based selection of province and district chiefs

Memorandum 002 gave the Republic a rural police, a Special Branch and province and district chiefs chosen by examination, on the same day as the land reform. Together with 001 they made a government in the district four to five years early: chiefs from the list held their districts through the coups, constables lived beside the Popular Forces, and the infrastructure in the government's own belt was driven out before Tet, as Operation NIGHT LANTERN showed in Can Giuoc in 1966. The costs came as predicted: constables killed in posts settled ahead of security, a war on the best chiefs, Ky's capture of the police against the Buddhists, and in Hue the Republic's own census turned into execution lists. Thieu captured the Board as the American lever lapsed, and the historical police closed the gap after 1969. The main-force war, Tet's verdict in Washington, the Easter Offensive and the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 stand. The end state stays at rung (a): the political deficit is now largely met where the government holds the night, and the conventional one is untouched.

## Memo 003 — Two U-2S Dragon Lady and four RQ-4B Global Hawk Block 40 high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft

Memorandum 003 gave this command two U-2S and four Global Hawks on the war's first day, and with them the first honest picture of the enemy's rear. The war's record moved; its outcome did not. The coastal radar closed the trawler route in 1964 and pushed the enemy's southern supply into Sihanoukville eighteen months early. On 4 August 1964 the Gulf watch saw no torpedo boats, Pierce Arrow was never flown, and the war's only legislative authority rested on the real attack of 2 August. From 1965 the Trail, the North's roads and the Cambodian route were counted rather than guessed, so the bombing's failures and the inflated truck claims reached Washington in weeks rather than years. The radar mapped the 1970 incursion's caches and struck the 1972 armour through cloud, but it deepened the fixation on Khe Sanh before Tet, saw nothing under the canopy or in the hamlets, and left with the Americans. Saigon still falls on 30 April 1975, at rung (a).

## Memo 004 — Modern infantry small arms for US, ARVN and RF/PF: M4A1 URG-I with Aimpoint CompM5, M110A2 squad marksman rifle, M249 squad automatic weapon

Memorandum 004 gave every American and South Vietnamese soldier and every territorial a modern carbine from 1964, with a belt-fed gun and a marksman in each regular squad. Its effect was concentrated where the war was decided first: at the outpost wall after dark. In the held belt a post with its platoon now held nine attacks in ten, and the land and police programmes had garrisons that won the first thirty seconds. The general reserve came through 1965 battered but whole, the M16 crisis of 1967 never happened, and at Tet a third of the attacks on the district towns failed at the walls. Perhaps 10,000–25,000 South Vietnamese and 1,000–2,500 American lives were saved, mostly before 1969, when the historical army caught up. Against this, the Front armed itself with our carbines, and the army that met the 1974 ration was more dependent on American ammunition and lost its hoards with I Corps. The enemy still chose every battle. Saigon falls on 30 April 1975, at rung (a).
